metadata.title: Claude, Legal Writing.
metadata.subtitle: A Harsher Reader, Never A Ghostwriter
metadata.purpose: Answer one real question in the Teardown register: does Claude grade your legal memo, or does it just write a better one for you? Lands the carry-out that legal-writing makes Claude a harsher reader, never a ghostwriter.

beats.narration_text: The obvious read: ask Claude for feedback on your memo, get a fixed memo back. Wrong branch — legal-writing is built to refuse the rewrite, on principle. Liam walks through what it does instead, and why the designers made that call.

beats.narration_text: Here's the design problem the skill has to solve at the door. In plain English, 'give me feedback on my memo' and 'fix this for me' collapse into the same request. That collision is exactly where the skill has to draw a line.

So the skill draws a hard line: no rewriting, ever. Ask it to rewrite anyway and it refuses, then offers three things it will do — structural feedback, one labeled example, or a drill on the underlying rule. The refusal isn't a preference, it's the design.

First move: read the whole draft top to bottom, no reactions yet — say, a 1L's memo arguing negligence in a car crash. Then name what it is: memo, brief, paper, or exam essay. That name isn't decoration — a memo grades against a different rubric than an exam essay.

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR — READS IT WHOLE FIRST
production_viz.caption: one running example: a 1L's negligence memo

beats.narration_text: Feedback then runs top-down: structure first, then whether the analysis actually connects rule to fact, then clarity and citation. The designers hard-coded that order because polishing sentences before the structure is fixed is wasted work — you'd be smoothing a house that's still crooked.

On structure it's confident — writing is writing, and a language model reads shape well. On whether the negligence rule is stated correctly, it won't guess: it flags VERIFY and hands the legal call back to you. That split is the model being honest about what it can and can't check.

shot.new_visual_element: CONFIDENT ON FORM, NOT ON LAW

production_viz.label: CONFIDENT ON FORM, NOT ON LAW
production_viz.caption: confident on form, not on law

beats.narration_text: Back to that same negligence memo: the skill might say the structure runs backwards, flag one rule to double-check, and stop. If it shows an example, it's one generic paragraph, labeled write yours, don't copy. That label is the whole design — everything short of writing the sentence for you.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR RETURNS — STILL NO REWRITE

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR RETURNS — STILL NO REWRITE
production_viz.caption: same memo, one example, never the paragraph itself

beats.narration_text: Two ways this catches you if you read the output lazily. A confident structural note doesn't prove the rule inside is correct — that's exactly what VERIFY is for. And a VERIFY flag doesn't mean the structure is fine, either. Both failure modes can live in the same paragraph.
Legal-writing's job is to make Claude a harsher reader of your memo, never its ghostwriter — the sentence still has to come from you.

props.quote: Legal-writing's job is to make Claude a harsher reader of your memo, never its ghostwriter — the sentence still has to come from you.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini: I'm working on a legal memo and I want you to be a harsher reader, not my ghostwriter. Don't rewrite any of it. Walk me through it in order: name the document type and pick the right rubric; grade the structure top-down; if you spot a legal rule stated in the memo — the elements of negligence, say — flag it VERIFY and tell me exactly what to double-check, don't guess whether it's correctly stated; then name the three highest-leverage fixes. If you show me an example paragraph, label it generic — write yours, don't copy. Go deeper: ask the same model to write you three paragraphs that pass a structural pass but each contain a subtly wrong legal rule — and see how easily you can spot which one is which.

llm_exercise.prompt: I'm working on a legal memo and I want you to be a harsher reader, not my ghostwriter. Here's the memo: [paste your memo]. Do not rewrite any of it. Walk me through it in this order: (1) name the document type — memo, brief, paper, exam essay — and grade it against the right rubric. (2) structural feedback top-down: is the organization sound, does the analysis apply the rule to the specific facts, does the conclusion follow. (3) if you spot a legal rule stated in the memo, flag it VERIFY and tell me exactly what to double-check; don't guess whether it's correctly stated. (4) name the three highest-leverage fixes. If you show me an example paragraph, label it 'generic — write yours, don't copy.'
